docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: Asked for on 2026-11-13: the whole of Rudolf OS as built so far converted to the native desktop. The shell first (docs/plan-1.6.0.md Part 12: everything the web desktop's shell has, Native the default), then every app rewritten as a native program, one at a time, in this plan. 2.0 is released when the apps in waves 1 to 3 are native. 2.0 also brings the phone's own build, on the hardware 1.6.1 proves ("The phone build", below).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13)
docs.t: Why (1.5.9's measurements, docs/plan-1.5.9.md 12.3a): with nothing open Native uses 854 MB against Standard's 1,110 MB, because no web page runs; each app opened today loads a WebKit page with the desktop's code (Settings: 195 MB). A native app of the same kind is typically 15 to 40 MB.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › How a native app is built
docs.t: C and GTK 3, as rudolf-native: the system layer already has GTK 3, cairo, Pango and GStreamer (for WebKitGTK), so most apps need no new library. A library an app would add (a PDF renderer, a source-code view) is named in its wave with its size, and the base layer's budget is checked by the release build as for ModemManager.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › How a native app is built
docs.t: One program per app (/usr/bin/rudolf-APP), started by rudolf-native as any program, framed by its window manager. A small shared library, librudolf-ui (iso/sys/ui/), holds what every app needs and the page already has: the accent colour and its variants (acVariant, acInk: already ported to C in rudolf-native), light and dark, the fonts and sizes of Display Properties, the translations (the page's language files read as they are), dialogs (Open, Save, Confirm in Rudolf's look), the about box, and rudolfd's client (the token, HTTP, JSON: from rudolf-native).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › How a native app is built
docs.t: Files: a native app reads and writes the account's real home folder (opened at sign-in by rudolfd), the same files the web apps see, so a document opened in WordLite's web version and in its native one is one file. Paths are shown as the page shows them (C:\\Users\\NAME\\Documents). Settings and an app's own state go through rudolfd (desktop/settings and a new apps/state?app=NAME), never into the web page's storage directly, so the page (Standard and Lite, still there) and native apps stay in step while both exist.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › How a native app is built
docs.t: The same look (the owner, 2026-11-14: Rudolf OS on Native appears and works exactly as on Standard): a native app is drawn to look like its web version, not like a stock GTK app: librudolf-ui carries a GTK CSS theme made from the page's styles (its buttons, fields, menus, scrollbars, tabs, lists, the accent colour, light and dark), and each app's windows are screenshot-compared with the web version as in docs/plan-1.6.0.md Part 12's rule (under 2 % of pixels different, text anti-aliasing aside). An app is not switched over until it passes.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › How a native app is built
docs.t: The same behaviour: each app's native version passes a checklist made from its web version (its menus, its shortcuts, its files, its settings, what its browser tests check), screenshots compared side by side under Xvfb. Until an app is native, its web version opens in a one-app WebKit window as in 1.6.0. When the native version passes, the start menu, the pins, file associations and Open with point to it; its web version stays in the page for Standard and Lite until 2.0 decides their future (below).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The order
docs.t: Small and much used first, so the way of building is proved on easy apps before the large ones. Wave 1: small apps, proving librudolf-ui Clock (alarms, timers, world clock), Calculator, Notepad, Task Manager (from rudolfd's process list, as now), Image Viewer, Screenshot, Characters & Emoji, Font Viewer, Trash.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The order
docs.t: Wave 2: the everyday tools File Explorer (its drag and drop with the shell's desktop and windows), Media Player (GStreamer), PDF Viewer (with printing, as 1.5.9's: a PDF renderer is the wave's one new library, poppler-glib, about 5 MB, budget checked), Archive Manager, Command Prompt and Terminal (VTE if it fits the budget, else a terminal of our own on a pty), Code Editor, Event Viewer, Calendar, Contacts, Weather, Voice Recorder, Camera, Help.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The order
docs.t: Wave 3: the large apps Settings (every page, Search in Settings with its index, Display Properties' previews drawn natively), WordLite, WordPro, SpreadsheetPro, PresentPro, Paint, App Store and Packages, Developer Console, Blitzen, Phone screen. Settings goes first in this wave: it is opened most, and its page costs the most memory today. Staying web pages (decided per app, not rewritten by default) Oracle Browser: a browser is a web engine; it stays Chromium (Standard) or WebKit, framed by the native window manager, its tabs and menus already its own.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The order
docs.t: The games and creative tools built on the web: Board Games, Card Games, Emu, Flash Player, Quake Engine, GPU Lab, WOS Galaxy Map, BlockLua Builder, and the screen savers: they draw with canvas and WebGL, a native rewrite gains little, and they open in one-app windows. Each is reconsidered after wave 3 with its memory measured.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Each app's pull request
docs.t: One app per pull request (a large app may take several, each one working), based on main, the owner merging: the program, its host test under Xvfb (iso/qt/native/APP_t.sh: opens, its checklist, screenshots), the start menu and associations switched once it passes, a CHANGELOG line, and its memory at idle with a file open measured against its web version (the PR says both). The release build compiles every native app and fails if one is missing from the base layer or over its budget.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › What 2.0 decides when wave 3 is done
docs.t: Whether Standard and Lite (the web desktop) stay in the system layer as fallbacks, or move to a recovery-only role, or go. Until then they stay, and Native gives up to Standard as in 1.5.9. Whether the web desktop is kept as the browser build (Rudolf OS in a browser tab) and the phone web app, or retired. Wayland (docs/plan-1.5.9.md 12.2: X11 for now): planned below ("Wayland", added on 2026-11-15); its switch for new installations is decided at its stage W5.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Measurements that close 2.0
docs.t: On the Vivobook, at idle and with the five most used apps open: memory used, start to the desktop, power on battery; against 1.5.9's table. Target: idle under 700 MB used, five apps open under 1 GB.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Wayland (added on 2026-11-15)
docs.t: Asked for on 2026-11-15: "Plan the Wayland migration for 2.0", after comparing Wayland with X11 for Rudolf OS. The recommendation then: X11 through 1.6.x (Native finished, several monitors with RandR as docs/plan-1.6.1.md Part 1 says, cellular), Wayland in 2.0 with the native apps and the mobile build.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Wayland (added on 2026-11-15)
docs.t: Why: apps of one account can no longer read each other's windows and keystrokes or send each other input (on X11 any client of the display can); tear-free drawing; per-display and fractional scaling; touch, gestures and the on-screen keyboard as the phone and tablet need them (every Linux phone shell is Wayland); several monitors of different sizes. Memory: about the same as X11 (the compositor replaces Xorg; Xwayland only while an X11 app runs), to be measured (W0).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Wayland (added on 2026-11-15)
docs.t: What stays the same: the owner's rule: Rudolf OS on Wayland appears and works exactly as on X11 (and as Standard), checked the same way (same_t.sh's screenshots, the behaviour scripts). Accounts, files, rudolfd, updates, recovery and the security model do not change. Standard, Lite and Native all run on it; X11 stays as a fallback session.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Wayland (added on 2026-11-15) › What changes, part by part
docs.t: The compositor: rudolf-native becomes it, built on wlroots (C, as rudolf-native; small; used by Sway, labwc, Phosh's phoc). It takes over what Xorg, rudolf-display and the window manager do today: outputs (DRM/KMS), input (libinput), focus, the windows' frames and stacking, workspaces, full screen. The shell's own surfaces (taskbar, start menu, tray pop-ups, notifications, the lock screen, the screen saver) are layer-shell surfaces of GTK 3 with gtk-layer-shell, drawn as now, so they look the same.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Wayland (added on 2026-11-15) › What changes, part by part
docs.t: rudolf-display's jobs move into the compositor: keyboard and pointer, the brightness and volume keys, the idle count (ext-idle-notify), the screen turning off, and the emergency keys (Ctrl+Alt+Backspace held: the safe desktop), which must keep working when the shell hangs: a small watchdog outside the compositor reads them from the kernel's input as rudolf-display does today, and restarts the session. The screen lock: ext-session-lock, so a crashing shell can never leave the desktop unlocked. Several monitors: docs/plan-1.6.1.md Part 1's design (a workspace per display) carried over to wlroots' outputs; per-display scaling (125 %, 150 %) added.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Wayland (added on 2026-11-15) › What changes, part by part
docs.t: Chromium (Standard's desktop, Oracle, its Tor windows): Chromium on Wayland (--ozone-platform=wayland); the shell in Chromium (the Isolated Web App, real tabs) checked unchanged. WebKit (Lite and the one-app windows): WebKitGTK on Wayland. X11 apps: Xwayland, started when the first X11 app opens and stopped after the last: Wine programs, Steam and its games, older Linux apps. Each account gets its own Xwayland (its own display and authority), as each account has its own display access on X11 today (1.5.9 15.3).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Wayland (added on 2026-11-15) › What changes, part by part
docs.t: Linux apps: Flatpak apps get the account's Wayland socket (and Xwayland's when they ask for X11); Debian's programs the same through rudolf-debian. Each account its own Wayland socket, readable by its own Linux user only. through the compositor (wlr-screencopy, and the ScreenCast portal over PipeWire for apps). rudolf-portal answers ScreenCast and RemoteDesktop as it answers the other portals, asking the person as the desktop asks today; remote access's input goes through the virtual keyboard and pointer protocols (or libei). Global shortcuts for apps: the GlobalShortcuts portal (rudolf-portal). Game mode, full screen, the controllers: unchanged in rudolfd; the compositor's full screen and direct scan-out for games (lower latency on the Vivobook's GPU).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Wayland (added on 2026-11-15) › What changes, part by part
docs.t: The on-screen keyboard and tablet mode: input-method and virtual-keyboard protocols, so the keyboard types into every app, Xwayland's included. Packages: wlroots, Xwayland, gtk-layer-shell, xdg-desktop-portal's pieces Rudolf does not answer itself: their sizes printed in the release build.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Wayland (added on 2026-11-15) › Tests
docs.t: The host tests that use Xvfb, xdotool and ImageMagick's import get Wayland equivalents: the compositor's headless backend (WLR_BACKENDS=headless) for a screen, wlrctl or the virtual input protocols for input, grim (screencopy) for screenshots. same_t.sh compares X11 and Wayland screens as it compares Native and Standard. QEMU (the t160 harness): a Wayland session starts, signs in, the account's apps get its Wayland socket and not another account's, Xwayland starts for a Wine program and stops after, the lock holds when the shell is killed. Each part's checks run on both sessions until X11 is retired.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Wayland (added on 2026-11-15) › Stages
docs.t: W0, measure and decide (before any code): on the Vivobook, a wlroots compositor with the desktop in it against today's X11: memory at idle, with Oracle, with a Wine program (Xwayland), start to the desktop, battery; Chromium, WebKitGTK, Steam, Wine, Flatpak apps and the calls sites checked on Wayland; written into this plan with a go or no-go for W1. W1, the compositor: rudolf-native as a wlroots compositor showing Native's shell exactly as on X11, as a test session (Settings › System health › Display: Wayland (test)), falling back to X11 by itself if it does not start, as Native falls back to Standard today.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Wayland (added on 2026-11-15) › Stages
docs.t: W2, the system around it: input, the idle count, the lock, the emergency keys' watchdog, several monitors, the W3, the apps: Chromium and WebKit on Wayland, Xwayland per account, Flatpak and Debian, Wine and Steam, game mode, the on-screen keyboard; same_t.sh and the behaviour scripts passing on both sessions. W4, betas: Wayland the session of new installations in betas (as Native's week of betas in 1.6.0); updated computers keep X11 and get the choice in Settings. W5, the switch: decided by the owner after the betas; X11 kept as the fallback session for at least two releases, then reconsidered. The mobile build is Wayland from its start.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › Wayland (added on 2026-11-15) › Order with the rest of 2.0
docs.t: W0 can run at any time (it changes nothing). W1 to W3 come after wave 1 (librudolf-ui proved), so the native apps are written once for both sessions, and alongside wave 2. W4 and W5 with wave 3's end, before 2.0's closing measurements.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The newest kernel and the "next" channel (added on 2026-11-20)
docs.t: The owner, 2026-11-20, after asking which kernel suits a high-end machine with Wayland, and whether mobile development can be done on 1.6's 6.18 LTS with X11 and also on a 7.3 build with Wayland: "Keep the 7.3 kernel development and Wayland as 2.0 items. Add everything else to 1.6.1."

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The newest kernel and the "next" channel (added on 2026-11-20)
docs.t: Two kernel tracks. 1.6.x stays on the 6.18 longterm kernel (the newest LTS, grep '^6\.18\.' in rudolf-release.yml): everyday and older computers, the recovery system. 2.0's work runs on the newest stable kernel (7.3.x on 2026-11-20, then 7.4 once it has settled): newer graphics drivers (7.2: AMD HDMI 2.1 FRL, Intel Arc; 7.3: NVK video decode, Valve's AMD reset and memory work), new hardware earlier, the 2026 Steam Controller and MSI Claw drivers, and the Wayland compositors' HDR and variable-refresh needs.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The newest kernel and the "next" channel (added on 2026-11-20)
docs.t: The "next" channel. A third release channel beside stable and beta (gh-pages next/, its own manifest, signed with the same keys, joined the way beta is joined in Settings › Update and recovery). Built by the same workflow with two switches: the kernel track (LTS or newest stable) and the session started by default (X11 or Wayland). Recovery mode stays the official stable release (the owner's rule), so a computer on "next" always has its way back.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The newest kernel and the "next" channel (added on 2026-11-20)
docs.t: What "next" carries, in order: first the newest kernel with X11 and the Wayland test session (W1, "Display: Wayland (test)"); then W2 and W3 as they land; Wayland by default there once W3 passes (before W4's betas on beta and stable). The kernel options for it: full preemption (preempt=full), 1000 Hz, sched_ext (a gaming scheduler such as scx_lavd loadable), NTSYNC for Proton, the newest firmware; measured as docs/plan-1.6.1.md Part 12 measures. The phone: stage 1 (its hardware, docs/plan-1.6.1.md Part 4) is done on 1.6's ARM64 build; the phone's own build and its interface (stage 2, below) are built on "next", Wayland from the start. The newer kernel helps the phones' own support (the PinePhone Pro, the Snapdragon 845 phones).

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The newest kernel and the "next" channel (added on 2026-11-20)
docs.t: NVIDIA's own driver (docs/plan-1.6.1.md Part 19), on "next": its module must build against each new kernel; the channel takes a new kernel only once it does (as Bazzite does), and says so in the build's notes. The cost: two release builds and two versions to test; the owner's rule for every session (same_t.sh's screenshots and the behaviour scripts) runs on both tracks. Order: the channel and the kernel switch first (nothing else changes for stable and beta); W0 measured on it; then the Wayland stages as above. When 2.0 is released, "next" becomes stable and 1.6.x keeps the LTS for older computers for at least two releases.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The phone build (added on 2026-11-15)
docs.t: Decided on 2026-11-15 (docs/plan-1.6.1.md, "The phone, split in two"): the phone comes in two stages. Stage 1, in 1.6.1, makes one ARM64 phone's hardware work under today's native desktop (the modem's data, texts and calls, emergency calls checked, the call's sound, sleep with the modem waking it, the battery). Stage 2, here, is the phone people can carry: Rudolf OS's own phone interface, built once for Wayland and the native apps, so it is never written for X11 and the web pages first and then again. The owner's rule holds: the phone's apps look and work as their desktop versions do, laid out for a small touch screen.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The phone build (added on 2026-11-15)
docs.t: Why it waits for 2.0: Wayland handles what a phone needs (touch gestures, rotation, scaling for a small sharp screen, the input method for the on-screen keyboard, drawing only what changes, which saves power), and the native apps fit a phone's memory and battery (a web app today: Settings 195 MB; a native one 15 to 40 MB). The phone build is Wayland from its start (W1 to W3 below) and uses the native apps as each wave makes them.

docs.h: Rudolf OS 2.0: the apps become native (added on 2026-11-13) › The phone build (added on 2026-11-15) › What it has
docs.t: The phone's own apps, native from the start (built with librudolf-ui's touch layouts): Phone (the dialler, calls, call history, voicemail, the in-call screen with the earpiece, speaker, headset and Bluetooth, the keypad, hold and two calls, emergency calls as 1.6.1 checked them), Messages (1.6.0's texts and picture messages, now native), Contacts. They come before wave 2's other apps on the phone. The desktop's native apps on the phone: each wave's app gets a touch layout in librudolf-ui (bigger targets, one column, its menus as a sheet), checked on the phone's screen size as each is checked against its web version: Clock, Calculator, Notepad, Settings, File Explorer, Media Player, Camera, Weather, Calendar, Help first.

docs.t: The on-screen keyboard as the Wayland input method (zwp_input_method_v2), in every app, Oracle and Linux apps included, with the account's language. The camera and sensors used: the Camera app with libcamera (photos and video, front and back), auto-rotation, the screen off at the ear during a call (proximity), auto-brightness, GPS for maps and weather, vibration for calls and notifications. Battery: suspend whenever the screen is off and nothing holds it, the modem waking it for calls and texts, apps in the background held back (as Android's Doze), measured against the same phone on Android (docs/plan-1.6.1.md Part 6), with targets set from 1.6.1's measurements.

docs.h: Rudolf OS games: a plan (asked for on 2026-11-11)
docs.t: Games made for Rudolf OS, published in the Rudolf OS Library (merciless146/rudolfos-library) and installed from the App Store. They are played first on Rudolf OS computers (keyboard, mouse, controllers), and every one is built so that it runs unchanged on the 1.6.0 mobile version (touch, portrait screens, ARM64, little memory), as all of Rudolf OS's own apps are to. Rudolf OS already has: Checkers and Chess (Board Games), Five-Card Draw, Texas Hold'em, Pai Gow Poker, Hearts and Solitaire (Card Games), Snake, Quake and the emulators (Library), the WOS Galaxy Map, BlockLua, and cloud gaming (Xbox Cloud Gaming, GeForce NOW). These games fill what is missing.

docs.h: Rudolf OS games: a plan (asked for on 2026-11-11) › Where they live
docs.t: The code: each game is a webapp package in rudolfos-library (apps/rudolf-<game>/PKGINFO and www/), built, signed with the Library's key and published by its workflow like rudolf-quake and rudolf-emu. Installed, it is mounted at /pkg/rudolf-<game>/ and served by rudolfd; removing it deletes one file. In the system (RudolfOS): a few lines per game, the Start menu and the App Store's Games tab entry with its icon, title and size. Opened without its package, it offers to download it, as Quake does. The system download does not grow with games. This plan: in RudolfOS (docs/plan-games.md), with the version plans.

docs.h: Rudolf OS games: a plan (asked for on 2026-11-11) › Rules for every game (desktop now, mobile in 1.6.0)
docs.t: 1. One input layer (a small shared library in the Library, rudolf-gamekit): keyboard, mouse, touch and gamepad at once, mapped to the game's actions. A game never assumes a mouse or a keyboard; on-screen controls appear only when touch is used. 2. Any window shape: the playfield scales to the window, portrait included (tablet mode, 1.5.8; phones, 1.6.0). 3. Speed: 60 frames a second drawn by the processor alone, Canvas 2D, no graphics card needed. The yardstick is the Vivobook on the Lite desktop (WebKit, software drawing). The same code on Chromium and WebKit. 4. Size: under about 2 MB per game, everything inside the package; nothing downloaded while playing.

docs.h: Rudolf OS games: a plan (asked for on 2026-11-11) › Rules for every game (desktop now, mobile in 1.6.0)
docs.t: 5. Saves: through rudolfd's mirror (they follow the account and are backed up), with export and import as a file. 6. Pausing: on the lock screen, the screen saver, a call (1.5.9 Part 7), a notification the person opens, the window covered or minimised, and on a phone when the app goes to the background. 7. Offline: everything works without a connection; online leaderboards only where a game has them, and optional. 8. Accessibility: difficulty levels, a reduce-flashing setting, colours that do not rely on red and green alone, remappable keys and buttons, captions for any spoken or important sound.

docs.h: Rudolf OS games: a plan (asked for on 2026-11-11) › The games › Night Flight (the only Christmas-themed game)
docs.t: A top-down, vertically scrolling bullet-hell shooter. Rudolf, the OS's mascot, flies up through a portrait playfield and fires lasers from his nose. Play Nose laser: tap or hold to fire a rapid stream; hold longer to charge a piercing beam. "Glow" pick-ups upgrade it (wider spread, then homing shots). Focus: hold a key (or a second finger) to move slowly; Rudolf's small hitbox, a glowing point at his nose, shows, for threading through dense patterns. Glow Burst (the bomb): a few per life; clears the bullets on screen and briefly turns corrupted enemies back to their colours. Grazing: passing close to bullets fills a meter for score and extra bombs.

docs.h: Rudolf OS games: a plan (asked for on 2026-11-11) › The games › Night Flight (the only Christmas-themed game)
docs.t: Bosses: one at the end of each stage, with phases and named bullet patterns. Rescues: corrupted friends can be saved (hit with a Glow Burst or the charged beam) for bonuses and extra lives. Modes: Story (6 stages), Practice (any stage reached, slow-motion assist), Score Attack, and after the ending a lighter "Restored" mode. The light-to-dark arc 1. Stages 1-2: a bright, colourful winter night: twinkling lights, candy colours, friendly villagers and workshop helpers. The first corrupted enemies are few and easy to read against the colour. 2. Stages 3-4: the corruption spreads: colours drain, lights flicker and glitch, friends begin to turn.

docs.h: Rudolf OS games: a plan (asked for on 2026-11-11) › The games › Night Flight (the only Christmas-themed game)
docs.t: 3. Stages 5-6: dark and corrupted: deep purples and blacks, static, inverted ornaments, cracked toys and twisted machinery, bullets in sickly glowing colours; the final boss is the source of the corruption. Clearing the game brings the colour back to every stage. Art direction

docs.h: Rudolf OS games: a plan (asked for on 2026-11-11) › The games › Night Flight (the only Christmas-themed game)
docs.t: Rudolf and the friendly characters: soft and cartoonish, child-friendly, in the spirit of open-source mascots such as Linux's Tux (without copying any of them): round shapes built from circles and ovals, no sharp corners; a big head and a small chubby body, short legs, stubby antlers with rounded tips; large friendly eyes with highlights, a small smile; Rudolf's nose glows warmly and pulses brighter as the laser charges. A few flat, warm, bright colours, a soft outline, one highlight and one shadow tone. Bouncy, squashy animation: Rudolf wobbles as he dodges, blinks, and cheers when a friend is rescued. Villagers, workshop helpers and small woodland animals in the same style.

docs.h: Rudolf OS games: a plan (asked for on 2026-11-11) › The games › Night Flight (the only Christmas-themed game)
docs.t: Corrupted characters: sinister, still simple enough to read at speed: angular and jagged silhouettes, cracks, thorny edges, uneven limbs; narrow glowing eyes (toxic purple, red or green) without highlights; dark, desaturated bodies with sickly glowing accents, flickering static and "corruption" dripping at the edges; jerky, glitching animation. A turning friend changes step by step from the round, colourful version to the sharp, dark one, and pops back when rescued, so the corruption is seen, not told. Child-friendly: creepy, not gory: no blood, nothing grotesque; beaten enemies burst into sparkles and static; bosses are menacing by shape, size and colour, not violence. The reduce-flashing setting tones the glitch effects down.

docs.h: Rudolf OS games: a plan (asked for on 2026-11-11) › The games › Night Flight (the only Christmas-themed game)
docs.t: Rudolf's own design: Rudolf is Rudolf OS's own character. Kept clearly distinct from Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer (a trademarked character): Rudolf OS's own antler shape, colours, proportions and style, and nothing from that story (Santa's reindeer team, its well-known characters, songs or places). The nose laser is a mechanic, not a borrowing. Worth a check by someone qualified before the game is published. Controls Desktop: arrows or WASD to move, Z to fire (hold to charge), Shift for focus, X for Glow Burst, Esc to pause; a controller (left stick or d-pad, A fire, right trigger focus, B bomb).

docs.h: Rudolf OS games: a plan (asked for on 2026-11-11) › The games › Night Flight (the only Christmas-themed game)
docs.t: Phone (1.6.0): drag anywhere to steer (Rudolf follows the finger at an offset, so the finger does not hide him), fire is automatic, a second finger held for focus, a two-finger tap for Glow Burst. Technical Canvas 2D; bullets in fixed pools (no allocation while playing); circle hit tests; a fixed time step, so runs are deterministic and replays can be saved and watched. Up to about 600 bullets on screen on the Vivobook on Lite; more where the computer allows (measured at start-up and in the settings). The corruption effects (palette shifts, scanlines, glitch slices) drawn cheaply in Canvas; none needs a graphics card.

docs.h: Rudolf OS games: a plan (asked for on 2026-11-11) › Progress
docs.t: 2026-11-12: Block Drop (apps/rudolf-blockdrop, about 20 KB as a package). Its own rules and look, not a copy of a trademarked game: an 8-wide, 16-deep well; pieces of three and four blocks; colours that do not follow the shape, each with its own mark (circle, triangle, square, diamond, cross). The twist: every 12th piece carries a prism; where it lands, every block of its colour bursts, the blocks above tumble down their columns, and rows that fill clear in a chain (worth more each step); while it falls, the blocks it would burst are outlined. Classic (faster every 10 rows), Relaxed (one speed), Daily (3 minutes, the same blocks for everyone). Touch: drag to move, tap to turn, flick down to drop, and a touch bar; on a tall window the panel moves above the well. tests/blockdrop_t.js (33 checks). In LIB_GAMES. Next: Logic Pack.

Sudoku Easy solves with naked singles, Medium with hidden singles too, Hard is only unique; Picture Grid 5×5, 10×10, 15×15, solvable line by line (a cell is given where line logic stalls); Cages 4×4 to 6×6. A Daily puzzle per kind. Notes, undo, clashes and wrong cages marked (with a bar, not colour alone), clues greyed when their line matches, hints that fix a wrong entry or do the next step and say why; each kind's puzzle in progress kept. The pad goes under the grid on a tall window. tests/logicpack_t.js (41 checks). In LIB_GAMES. Next (1.5.9-1.6.0): Wordsmith, Galaxy Conquest, FreeCell and Spider, Chess levels.

docs.h: Rudolf OS games: a plan (asked for on 2026-11-11) › Frost Barricade 1.1: twenty-five nights, the weather radio, the weather, wendigos
docs.t: Asked for on 2026-11-11 and built (rudolfos-library#6, on #5's eye colours, bloaters and muggers). Twenty-five nights; the sleigh comes at the end of the last, in the great blizzard. A prep screen before every night with a weather radio: tonight's weather and tomorrow night's, a warning the day before a blizzard, and on Day 22 always the warning of the three-night blizzard. The schedule, fixed per game from its seed: days 1-7 clear or fog; a blizzard on day 8 or 9 and on 17 or 18 (the other day clear or fog); the great blizzard on 23-25; one full moon (20% a day on days 8-14, 60% on 15-20, 80% on 21, otherwise 22), never on a blizzard's day.

docs.h: Rudolf OS games: a plan (asked for on 2026-11-11) › Frost Barricade 1.1: twenty-five nights, the weather radio, the weather, wendigos
docs.t: Clear: full sight; searching goes quicker. Full moon: brighter; every white-eyed elf becomes a red-eyed sprinter; a wendigo comes. Fog: sight is a cone of light from Rudolf's nose towards the crosshair; elves out of it show as ripples of sound; their sounds louder; searching finds less and scouts are more often lost. Blizzard: a shorter, narrower cone; no ripples; nothing sprints; the survivors' aim suffers; no searching.

docs.h: Rudolf OS games: a plan (asked for on 2026-11-11) › Frost Barricade 1.1: twenty-five nights, the weather radio, the weather, wendigos
docs.t: The wendigo (reworked in 1.2): a mini-boss, always red-eyed; a screech (and a caption) a few seconds before it appears; huge, very tough and slow, drifting towards Rudolf's lane; only one on the field at a time. Every 5-8 s it stops for 1.5 s to draw in a screech, then lets it go down its lane with the screen shaking: it hurts survivors in its path (not the barricade), and if it reaches Rudolf he is stunned, his sight blurs and his ears ring, fully for 3 s, then fading. One under the full moon, one on Night 24, two on Night 25 (one after the other). An original design: gaunt, long-limbed, sharp branching antlers, frightening by shape rather than gore.

Their shield covers the waist, chest and head (not the lower legs and feet) and stops every shot, survivors' bolts included; piercing shots stop at it; fire reaches round it for half. Explosives and Bash knock it loose and the shielder back. From Night 10 a shielder goes back for its own shield; from Night 18 an ordinary white-eyed elf walking over a fallen shielder's shield may take it up (it keeps its white eyes and its own health).

docs.h: The Rudolf OS Library: a catalog of apps made for Rudolf OS (planned for 1.5.2) › How it works: rpk, which Rudolf OS already has
docs.t: rpk (iso/sys/rpk.c) is Rudolf OS's package manager since 1.3.0: a package is a read-only squashfs image with an Ed25519 signature; installed packages are mounted at /pkg/<name>, so installing never changes the system and removing one deletes one file; kinds: webapp (www/ served by rudolfd at /pkg/<name>/, opened in a desktop window), addon (files the desktop uses), app, cli; a repository is static files: index.txt (one package per line) and index.sig, plus the packages; sources: the disc's own repository and lines in /persist/pkg/sources. The Library is an rpk repository on the internet, added to every computer's sources. Packages: rudolf-quake (addon): the files now in www/rudolfq, served at /pkg/rudolf-quake/www/; rudolf-emu (addon): the emulators now in www/lib/emu.

docs.h: The Rudolf OS Library: a catalog of apps made for Rudolf OS (planned for 1.5.2) › How it works: rpk, which Rudolf OS already has
docs.t: The desktop looks for them at /pkg/<name>/ instead of in its own folder.

docs.h: The Rudolf OS Library: a catalog of apps made for Rudolf OS (planned for 1.5.2) › Where it lives: a GitHub repository, yes, a separate one
docs.t: A GitHub repository is the right home, and a separate one, merciless146/rudolfos-library, is better than a folder in RudolfOS. Why GitHub: Hosting at no cost, and no server to run. The packages go in GitHub Releases (files up to 2 GB each), and the signed index in GitHub Pages. Rudolf OS's own updates already work this way, so nothing new needs to be learned or paid for. The host does not need to be trusted. rpk checks every package's signature against keys built into Rudolf OS, so a database server or anything more would add nothing. A build workflow (Actions) packs, signs and publishes each app, and keeps the history of every version. Why separate from RudolfOS:

docs.h: The Rudolf OS Library: a catalog of apps made for Rudolf OS (planned for 1.5.2) › Where it lives: a GitHub repository, yes, a separate one
docs.t: Its own schedule. A new version of an app is published by itself, without a Rudolf OS release, and every computer gets it through the App Store's updates. Its own key. See below: if the Library's key were ever stolen, it could not sign a system update. Room for others. People who make apps for Rudolf OS can later be given access to the Library repository without any access to the operating system or its keys. A clean RudolfOS repository, whose gh-pages branch holds only the system's update channels.

docs.h: The Rudolf OS Library: a catalog of apps made for Rudolf OS (planned for 1.5.2) › Where it lives: a GitHub repository, yes, a separate one
docs.t: Layout of rudolfos-library: ` apps/<name>/PKGINFO name, version, kind, title, description, icon, licence, category apps/<name>/www/... the app's files (or a fetch script for large data, pinned by SHA-256) .github/workflows/publish.yml build each changed app, sign it, upload it to a release, update the signed index ` Published: https://merciless146.github.io/rudolfos-library/index.txt, index.sig and catalog.json (titles, icons, descriptions, sizes, for the App Store), with the packages next to them (<name>.rpk). (As built: rpk takes each package's file from the same place as the list, so the packages are on Pages too, not in Releases.)

docs.h: The Rudolf OS Library: a catalog of apps made for Rudolf OS (planned for 1.5.2) › Keys: the Library gets its own
docs.t: Today /etc/rudolf/rpk-keys is trusted by both rpk (packages) and rudolf-update (the system's updates). A key added there for the Library could also sign a system update. So: a new Ed25519 key pair for the Library, made by you with the existing tool (as the release key was); its public key in a new file, /etc/rudolf/library-keys, which rpk trusts and rudolf-update does not. The release key keeps signing system updates only.

docs.h: The Rudolf OS Library: a catalog of apps made for Rudolf OS (planned for 1.5.2) › The App Store and the desktop
docs.t: A Rudolf OS Library tab in the App Store: each app with its icon, size, description and licence, and Get / Open / Remove / Update. Opening Quake or Emu without the package: "Quake is in the Rudolf OS Library (13 MB). Download it?", and it opens when the download finishes. Nobody loses an app: on the first start of 1.5.2, a computer whose Games folder or saves show it used Quake or Emu gets that package installed by itself (in the background, when online), with a notification.

The download of the system shrinks, and the disc stays the same size. Updates: the App Store's Updates also checks the Library; the health log records installs and updates.

docs.h: Finding the hidden memory: one start without lockdown (planned 2026-11-12)
docs.t: Why: on the Vivobook (3.4 GB, AMD 0x1506), Standard at idle uses about 1.0 to 1.2 GB, and about 200 to 250 MB of it belongs to no process (docs/plan-1.5.9.md Part 10). On budget and old computers that is a large share. The only place that says what it is, is the kernel's debug files (debugfs): the graphics driver's page pool, every graphics buffer with the process that owns it, and the buffers shared between processes. With Secure Boot on, the start-up locks the kernel down (integrity), and lockdown keeps debugfs closed. So the reading needs one start with Secure Boot off, then Secure Boot back on. Nothing in Rudolf OS changes for it, and no release ever ships without lockdown.

docs.h: Finding the hidden memory: one start without lockdown (planned 2026-11-12) › What is safe about it, and what is given up for that start
docs.t: Turning Secure Boot off in the firmware keeps the Rudolf OS key: it is in shim's key list (MOK), not the firmware's own keys. Rudolf OS starts as before (docs/secure-boot.md: "With Secure Boot off everything works as before, and the layers are still checked"). For that one start: unsigned kernel modules and kernels could load, and kernel memory could be read or written by root. Nothing does that in Rudolf OS, but the start should do nothing else: no browsing, no downloads, no USB script below, which reads.

docs.h: Finding the hidden memory: one start without lockdown (planned 2026-11-12) › What is safe about it, and what is given up for that start
docs.t: Never choose "Reset to setup mode", "Clear Secure Boot keys" or "Restore factory keys" in the firmware: that could remove the keys the firmware checks shim with. Only the one switch, Secure Boot on/off. The test-only start options (RUDOLF_UKI_TEST_CMDLINE and the test keys) are not used: the release's own signed start, with Secure Boot off, is all that is needed.

docs.h: Finding the hidden memory: one start without lockdown (planned 2026-11-12) › Steps
docs.t: 1. Before (Secure Boot on): the final 1.5.8 installed, Standard, signed in, nothing open, five minutes idle. The usual read (memgap.sh) for the baseline: the in-use figure, the processes, the gap. 2. Secure Boot off: restart into the firmware (on Asus laptops usually F2 at the logo, then Advanced mode › Security › Secure Boot › Secure Boot Control: Disabled), save and restart. Sign in, open nothing, five minutes idle. 3. Check the start: lockdown reads [none] and the gap is about the same as in step 1 (the same start, only unlocked). If the gap is very different, the comparison is off: stop and note it.

docs.h: Finding the hidden memory: one start without lockdown (planned 2026-11-12) › Steps
docs.t: 4. Read, three times (memdbg.sh, read-only: it mounts debugfs read-only, reads, unmounts): - idle: as it is; - video: a YouTube video full screen in Oracle for two minutes, then the reading while it plays; - closed: the video's tab closed, two minutes, then the last reading (what stays after use). The script refuses to read anything if lockdown is on. 5. Secure Boot back on, the same switch: restart into the firmware, Secure Boot Control: Enabled, save, restart.

docs.h: Finding the hidden memory: one start without lockdown (planned 2026-11-12) › Steps
docs.t: 6. Check it is back: lockdown reads [integrity], /etc/rudolf/secureboot is 1, and Task Manager › System and Settings › Security say Secure Boot is on. If the computer does not start with it on, the key was lost: enroll it again (MokManager, docs/secure-boot.md), never leave it off. The whole start without lockdown takes about 20 minutes.

docs.h: Finding the hidden memory: one start without lockdown (planned 2026-11-12) › What is read
docs.t: TTM page pool (ttm/page_pool): pages the graphics driver keeps for reuse after buffers are freed. Counted as used, owned by no process. Graphics buffers by process (dri/*/amdgpu_gem_info): every buffer, in VRAM (the 256 MB carve-out) or in GTT (system memory the graphics card uses), with its owner: Chromium's GPU process, the compositor (cage), Xwayland. Memory managers (amdgpu_vram_mm, amdgpu_gtt_mm): how much of each is handed out. Shared buffers (dma_buf/bufinfo): buffers passed between processes (the screen's own, video frames). With them, as before: meminfo, slab, vmalloc by caller.

docs.h: Finding the hidden memory: one start without lockdown (planned 2026-11-12) › What each answer leads to
docs.t: | Where the gap is | What it means | What can be done (1.5.9 or later) | |---|---|---| | The TTM pool | freed graphics memory kept for reuse | cap the pool (ttm.page_pool_size) for small computers; measure the frame rate before and after | | GTT buffers of Chromium's GPU process | the desktop page's layers and textures | Part 10 (a lighter page), fewer layers (the overlays only when shown), Chromium's GPU memory limits | | GTT buffers of cage or Xwayland | the screen's buffers | fewer screen buffers (double rather than triple), Xwayland only when an X app runs | | Shared video buffers | frames kept after the video | check they are freed when the tab closes (the closed reading) | | Slab or vmalloc | the kernel itself | the driver or module named, and its options |

docs.h: Finding the hidden memory: one start without lockdown (planned 2026-11-12) › What each answer leads to
docs.t: The findings go into docs/plan-1.5.9.md (Part 10, or a new part), with the readings.

docs.h: Finding the hidden memory: one start without lockdown (planned 2026-11-12) › What the first reading found (2026-11-12, released 1.5.8, 2026111219)
docs.t: | Reading | In use | Unaccounted | Graphics pool (TTM) | Graphics in system memory (GTT) | |---|---|---|---|---| | idle | 1,074 MB | 198 MB | 21 MB | 17 MB | | a video full screen | 1,906 MB | 245 MB | 27 MB | 38 MB | | two minutes after closing Oracle | 1,228 MB | 206 MB | 46 MB | 19 MB | Graphics buffers are small (the X server about 27 MB, Chromium's GPU process 8 to 23 MB, mostly in the 256 MB of the graphics card's own memory); no shared buffers (dma-buf) at all.

docs.h: Finding the hidden memory: one start without lockdown (planned 2026-11-12) › What the first reading found (2026-11-12, released 1.5.8, 2026111219)
docs.t: The graphics pool grows a little with use (21 → 46 MB) and its limit is 1.7 GB: a cap (64 MB) goes into 1.5.9. 140 to 180 MB is neither graphics nor any counter: memory taken page by page by the kernel or a driver, there from the start and steady. This kernel has nothing that names it (no /proc/allocinfo, no page_owner).

docs.h: Finding the hidden memory: one start without lockdown (planned 2026-11-12) › Part 2: a test kernel that names it
docs.t: The workflow *Test kernel* (iso/systools/testkernel.sh) builds the stable release's kernel with allocation profiling (MEM_ALLOC_PROFILING, on from the start) and its own modules layer, as the pre-release test-allocinfo. No update ever installs it. On the Vivobook, with Secure Boot off again (the same switch): and its modules, and the base, Chromium and desktop layers of the running slot (hard links, no extra room). 2. The running system hands over to the test kernel (sync, file systems read-only, kexec with rudolf.slot=r): the same start as an update's, without the firmware. The modules layer is not the release's, so it starts as "unchecked", which only a start with Secure Boot off allows.

docs.h: Finding the hidden memory: one start without lockdown (planned 2026-11-12) › Part 2: a test kernel that names it
docs.t: 3. Five minutes idle, then /proc/allocinfo is read (read-only): every place in the kernel with how much it holds, the largest first, along with the counters above. 4. A normal restart (the released kernel again), the slot r removed, and Secure Boot back on and checked. Nothing else on the drive changes; if the test kernel does not start, the power button and a normal start bring the released system back.

docs.h: Finding the hidden memory: one start without lockdown (planned 2026-11-12) › What the test kernel found (2026-11-12, idle, 204 MB unaccounted)
docs.t: /proc/allocinfo on the Vivobook, five minutes idle (the test kernel through slot r, Secure Boot off): | Held by | MB | What it is | |---|---|---| | drivers/iommu/dma-iommu.c (__iommu_dma_alloc_pages) | 65 | the SSD's host memory buffer: the Kingston OM8PGP4128P has no DRAM of its own and borrows 64 MiB (nvme0: allocated 64 MiB host memory buffer) | | ttm_pool_alloc_page [ttm] | 42 | the graphics driver's pool and the graphics card's system memory | | net/core/skbuff.c (kmalloc_reserve) | 16 | network (Wi-Fi) receive buffers | | blk-mq requests, dm-bufio | 9 | the drive's requests; dm-verity's cache of checked blocks | | IOMMU tables, smaller | 5 | |

docs.h: Finding the hidden memory: one start without lockdown (planned 2026-11-12) › What the test kernel found (2026-11-12, idle, 204 MB unaccounted)
docs.t: About 135 of the 204 MB is named; the other 60 to 70 MB was taken before tracking could see it (early start-up). Nothing is a leak and nothing is wasted by Rudolf OS. The largest part is the hardware of a budget laptop: an SSD without DRAM borrows RAM, and it is faster for it. Limiting it (nvme.max_host_mem_size_mb) would trade the drive's speed for 64 MB: left as it is. The graphics pool cap stays in 1.5.9 (Part 10); the network and drive buffers are normal and small. The memory to win is the desktop page's (Part 10), not hidden memory.

docs.h: Finding the hidden memory: one start without lockdown (planned 2026-11-12) › What the test kernel found (2026-11-12, idle, 204 MB unaccounted)
docs.t: After the reading: a normal restart into the released kernel, slot r and the test files removed, Secure Boot back on and checked (lockdown [integrity], 2026111219 from slot b). The pre-release test-allocinfo stays for a later measurement; it is never in a channel. The test kernel's screen was garbled: handing over by kexec from a running desktop leaves the graphics card set up hand over before any graphics driver has started, so they are not affected.

docs.h: Oracle: find, closed tabs, passwords, blocking, reader mode and extensions (asked for on 2026-11-16)
docs.t: The owner compared Oracle with Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari and Brave on 2026-11-16 and asked for a plan for five of the improvements suggested then. "Create a plan for recommended items 1, 2, 4, 5, and 7": Item 1: find in page (Ctrl+F). Item 2: reopen a closed tab (Ctrl+Shift+T) and restore the last session. Item 4: a password manager for websites, kept in the account's keyring. Item 5: ad and tracker blocking. Item 7: reader mode. Item 6 (added the same day): extensions from a reviewed list in the Library.

docs.h: Oracle: find, closed tabs, passwords, blocking, reader mode and extensions (asked for on 2026-11-16)
docs.t: The parts below keep those numbers. The other items are not part of this plan: item 3 (no 12-tab limit), item 8 (pinned and muted tabs, tab search, the padlock, site permissions) and item 9 (export and import instead of sync).

docs.h: Oracle: find, closed tabs, passwords, blocking, reader mode and extensions (asked for on 2026-11-16) › Where Oracle's pages live (what each part must cover)
docs.t: Oracle shows a page in one of four ways. Every part below works in all four, on Standard and on Native, as the owner's rule says: "Rudolf OS on the native desktop should appear and function exactly as it does in Chromium mode."

docs.t: | Where | What it is | How Oracle reaches it | |---|---|---| | Real tabs (Standard and Native) | a controlledframe in the IWA shell (iso/shell/shell.js), Rudolf's Chromium | the shell's messages (tabs26.js ⇄ shell.js): executeScript, addContentScripts, request.createWebRequestInterceptor (already used by the firewall), and find/stopFinding | | Lite's tabs | WebKitGTK pages made by rudolf-webkit (oracle58.js) | the same messages; rudolf-webkit uses WebKitFindController, WebKitUserContentManager scripts and WebKitUserContentFilterStore | | The frames fallback | an iframe in the desktop page, when the shell is not running | only what an iframe allows: the page's own content cannot be reached, so these parts say so plainly or are left out | | Oracle's own pages | about: pages, files on C:, .HTM files, all srcdoc (base_v24.html page()) | a small script added to the page, as ORACLE_TEL_JS is today |

docs.t: Private and Tor windows (private59.js, tor59.js) keep nothing: no session, no closed-tab list after the window closes, no passwords saved (saved ones can still be filled, after a click), and no reader-mode history.

docs.h: Oracle: find, closed tabs, passwords, blocking, reader mode and extensions (asked for on 2026-11-16) › Item 1. Find in page
docs.t: What the person sees. Ctrl+F, F3, or ☰ › Find in page… opens a bar under the bookmarks bar. It has a text box, "3 of 17", up and down buttons, a "Match case" box and ✕. Enter goes to the next match, Shift+Enter to the previous one, Escape closes the bar, and the matches are highlighted as Chromium highlights them. Text selected on the page fills the box. The bar belongs to its tab: switching tabs hides it, and switching back shows it with the same text. How.

docs.h: Oracle: find, closed tabs, passwords, blocking, reader mode and extensions (asked for on 2026-11-16) › Item 1. Find in page
docs.t: Real tabs: controlledframe.find(text, {backward, matchCase}) and its findupdate event give the count and the current match; stopFinding('clear') when the bar closes. If Chromium 158's controlledframe lacks find, fall back to a script run with executeScript that walks the page's text (as below). Lite: rudolf-webkit's tab answers a new find message with webkit_find_controller_search and count_matches (WEBKIT_FIND_OPTIONS_WRAP_AROUND, CASE_INSENSITIVE unless "Match case"). Oracle's own pages: a script added to every srcdoc page, which marks matches with <mark> through a TreeWalker over text nodes (never innerHTML) and scrolls to the current one. Frames fallback: the bar says "Find is not available for this page" (the page is another site's frame).

docs.h: Oracle: find, closed tabs, passwords, blocking, reader mode and extensions (asked for on 2026-11-16) › Item 1. Find in page
docs.t: The keys. A page may take Ctrl+F for itself (Google Docs, VS Code for the web), so Oracle takes it first, as Chrome does. On Standard, rudolf-display hands Oracle's own keys to the desktop as Ctrl+F20–F23 (desk_key, 1.5.9). Ctrl+F and F3 join them, for Oracle's windows only. On Native, rudolf-native's key handling for Oracle's window does the same, as #434 did for Ctrl+W, T, N and Q. Tests. A shell2 browser test with a stand-in shell (as oracle58_t.js): the bar, the count, next and previous, Escape, Match case, and the bar following its tab. A test of the real shell in Chromium: a local test page with 17 matches gives "1 of 17" and moves to the next one.

docs.h: Oracle: find, closed tabs, passwords, blocking, reader mode and extensions (asked for on 2026-11-16) › Item 1. Find in page
docs.t: WebKit: the same with rudolf-webkit (oracle_native_t.sh's harness). The keys: Ctrl+F in a page that listens for it opens Oracle's bar on Standard and Native (dispkeys, tor_native_t.sh's way of sending keys). The owner's checks. Ctrl+F on a long page (a Wikipedia article) on Standard, Native and Lite; F3; Escape; Ctrl+F inside Google Docs (Oracle's bar opens, as in Chrome).

docs.h: Oracle: find, closed tabs, passwords, blocking, reader mode and extensions (asked for on 2026-11-16) › Item 2. Reopen a closed tab, and restore the last session
docs.t: What the person sees. Ctrl+Shift+T, or ☰ › Recently closed, reopens the last closed tab at its place, with its back and forward history. Pressed again, it reopens the one before. The list keeps the last 25 tabs, and a closed window counts as one entry that brings all its tabs back. ☰ › Recently closed lists them with their titles and sites. Settings › Oracle (or ☰ › Settings) › "When Oracle starts": - Open the start page (the default). - Continue where you left off: every Oracle window and its tabs as they were, each tab asleep (💤) until it is clicked, so starting is quick.

docs.h: Oracle: find, closed tabs, passwords, blocking, reader mode and extensions (asked for on 2026-11-16) › Item 2. Reopen a closed tab, and restore the last session
docs.t: After Oracle or the desktop ended unexpectedly (the memory guard, a crash, the power), the next Oracle window offers "Restore your tabs?" once, whatever the setting. How. tabs26.js and browser() keep a per-window list of closed tabs: the URL, its title, the history entries (t.h, t.i) and the zoom. Real tabs give their own history through the shell's back and forward events (t.rb, t.rf). The session (windows, tabs, the active tab) is saved in the account's storage, with Oracle's history and bookmarks, when a tab opens, closes or navigates (at most once a second). A clean exit marks it closed. On start, "continue" opens each tab asleep with the sleeping tabs' existing path (t.slept, rtOpen when shown).

docs.h: Oracle: find, closed tabs, passwords, blocking, reader mode and extensions (asked for on 2026-11-16) › Item 2. Reopen a closed tab, and restore the last session
docs.t: Never for private and Tor windows: their tabs go to an in-memory list that disappears with the window. On Native, each Oracle window is its own one-app page (oneapp59.js). The session is the account's, written by whichever window changed last. The native desktop starting Oracle at sign-in reads it once, so two windows never restore the same session twice. Tests. shell2: close three tabs, Ctrl+Shift+T three times (order, history, place); a closed window brings back its tabs. The session saved, the page reloaded, "continue" restoring windows and asleep tabs; "start page" not restoring. An unclean end offers "Restore your tabs?" once. A private window leaves nothing in storage.

docs.h: Oracle: find, closed tabs, passwords, blocking, reader mode and extensions (asked for on 2026-11-16) › Item 2. Reopen a closed tab, and restore the last session
docs.t: Native: two Oracle windows, the desktop restarted, both windows back once (host harness, same_oracle_t.sh). The owner's checks. Close a tab and press Ctrl+Shift+T on Standard and Native. Turn on "Continue where you left off", restart the Vivobook, and the tabs are back. A private window's tabs are not offered.

docs.h: Oracle: find, closed tabs, passwords, blocking, reader mode and extensions (asked for on 2026-11-16) › Item 4. A password manager for websites
docs.t: What the person sees. After signing in to a site, Oracle asks "Save your password for example.com?" with Save, Never for this site and Not now. On a sign-in form of a site with saved passwords, a key 🔑 appears in the password box. Clicking it, or the user name box, shows the saved accounts. Choosing one fills both boxes, and nothing is filled before the person chooses. On a sign-up or new-password form, the key offers "Use a strong password" (20 characters, generated by Rudolf), saved once the form is sent.

docs.h: Oracle: find, closed tabs, passwords, blocking, reader mode and extensions (asked for on 2026-11-16) › Item 4. A password manager for websites
docs.t: Where they are kept. In the signed-in account's keyring (1.6.0 Part 14, the Secret Service), in a collection of Oracle's own ("Oracle website passwords"), unlocked when the account signs in. Nothing is kept in the page's storage, localStorage or a file, and nothing leaves the computer: there is no sync in this plan. Removing the account removes them. How. rudolfd gets keyring endpoints for Oracle (as the account's own Linux user, as keyring/list does): pw/list gives sites and user names only; pw/get returns one password for an exact origin. pw/set, pw/del, pw/import and pw/export, with get, export and the Settings page's Show needing the account's password again, as elevation does today.

docs.h: Oracle: find, closed tabs, passwords, blocking, reader mode and extensions (asked for on 2026-11-16) › Item 4. A password manager for websites
docs.t: The page never sees the list. A content script in the tab (addContentScripts for real tabs, a WebKitUserContentManager script for Lite, both in an isolated world) finds password forms and tells Oracle the form's origin when it is submitted. Oracle, not the page, asks rudolfd, and only for the tab's own top-level origin (scheme, host and port exactly: never a parent domain, never http for an https entry, never inside a cross-origin iframe). The fill goes back to that one form by the content script, after the person's click. Never: filling on http:// pages without a warning, filling without a click, or saving from private and Tor windows. The frames fallback (no access to the page) is never filled.

Origin rules: https://a.example's entry not offered on http://a.example, sub.a.example, a.example:8443 or in an iframe of another site; a private window offers but never saves. Its menu shows "Blocking ads and trackers on example.com" with a switch to turn it off for this site, and "Report a broken site" (a note in the health log, nothing sent). docs.h: Oracle: find, closed tabs, passwords, blocking, reader mode and extensions (asked for on 2026-11-16) › Item 5. Ad and tracker blocking
docs.t: What it blocks. Network requests matching EasyList (ads) and EasyPrivacy (trackers), and the empty boxes left behind (element hiding). The lists are compiled at build time into a compact matcher (domains, URL patterns with their options: third-party, resource type, exceptions), and the page's hiding rules are applied as CSS. Licences: EasyList and EasyPrivacy are dual-licensed GPLv3+ / CC BY-SA 3.0. They are credited in About Oracle, with the list versions. How. Real tabs: the shell's existing request interceptor (request.createWebRequestInterceptor, which the firewall already uses for every request) checks the matcher next to the firewall's rule. The hiding CSS is added by addContentScripts at document-start: generic rules plus that site's rules.

docs.h: Oracle: find, closed tabs, passwords, blocking, reader mode and extensions (asked for on 2026-11-16) › Item 5. Ad and tracker blocking
docs.t: Lite: the same lists converted at build time to WebKit's content-blocker JSON, compiled once with WebKitUserContentFilterStore and added to each tab's content manager. This is WebKit's own fast path, as Safari uses. Frames fallback: not possible (another site's frame). The shield says so. Updates. The lists change weekly. They come with Rudolf's updates, and between updates as a signed list published with the Library (signed by the Library's key; never an unsigned download). The matcher keeps working with the list it has when there is no network.

docs.h: Oracle: find, closed tabs, passwords, blocking, reader mode and extensions (asked for on 2026-11-16) › Item 5. Ad and tracker blocking
docs.t: Speed. The interceptor answers in microseconds per request (a hash of domains, then a small set of patterns). Measure page loads with and without on the Vivobook. If the interceptor is too slow, the fallback is shipping uBlock Origin Lite (GPLv3, Manifest V3, declarativeNetRequest) as a built-in extension loaded as Ruffle's is (--load-extension), with Oracle's shield driving it. Item 6 also offers it as an extension of the person's choice. Tests. Host test of the compiler and matcher against EasyList's own syntax cases (exceptions, $third-party, $domain, separator ^).

A news site with ads on Standard, Native and Lite; the shield's count; turning it off for that site; YouTube, a bank's site and Google sign-in still working (the usual places a blocker breaks things).

docs.h: Oracle: find, closed tabs, passwords, blocking, reader mode and extensions (asked for on 2026-11-16) › Item 7. Reader mode
docs.t: What the person sees. On a page with an article (a news story, a blog post, a recipe), a 📖 button appears in the address box. Pressing it (or F9) shows the article alone: its title, author, date, text, pictures and links, in Rudolf's reading style. Style: the size (A− A+), the width, the font (sans, serif, OpenDyslexic when the account uses the dyslexia font), and the colours (light, sepia, dark; dark by default when Rudolf's dark theme is on). Read aloud: Rudolf's own voice (tts25.js), with the sentence being read highlighted. Leaving: "Exit reader" (or F9 again) goes back to the page as it was. Reader mode is per tab, and the address stays the page's. How.

docs.h: Oracle: find, closed tabs, passwords, blocking, reader mode and extensions (asked for on 2026-11-16) › Item 7. Reader mode
docs.t: Mozilla's Readability.js (Apache-2.0, credited in About Oracle) is run in the tab by Oracle (executeScript for real tabs, rudolf-webkit's script for Lite) when the page has loaded. Its isProbablyReaderable shows the button, and parse() returns the article. The article's HTML goes through safeHtml() (sanitize59.js: parsed inert, nothing that runs, links made plain) and is shown in an Oracle page of its own (about:reader?u=…, srcdoc, sandboxed, no scripts but Oracle's controls). Pictures are loaded from the site as the page did; nothing else is. Oracle's own pages and files: reader mode on a .HTM file on C: as well. Frames fallback: not available. Private and Tor windows: available; nothing is kept.

docs.h: Oracle: find, closed tabs, passwords, blocking, reader mode and extensions (asked for on 2026-11-16) › Item 7. Reader mode
docs.t: Printing from reader mode prints the article alone (print25.js), which is the most common reason people want it. Tests. shell2: a local article page shows the button and a plain page does not; the article's title and text are right; scripts and event handlers in the article never run (an onerror and a <script> in the test page). The size, font and dark settings, read aloud starting, exit restoring the page. htmlsinks reviewed (the article is HTML from data: through safeHtml only). Lite: the same with rudolf-webkit. The owner's checks. A long news article on Standard, Native and Lite: the button, the article, A+, dark, read aloud, print, exit.

On the recommendation, the owner said: "Use the recommendation provided above to add item #6 from the list to the plan." The source: Rudolf's own reviewed list, in the Library. Each extension is an open-source Manifest V3 extension. It is built from its published source by rudolfos-library's workflow, signed with the Library's key, and listed in the App Store under "Oracle extensions". Oracle installs only extensions from that list. Each one has a stated licence, a pinned version, a review of its permissions, and updates through the Library. The first five:

docs.h: Oracle: find, closed tabs, passwords, blocking, reader mode and extensions (asked for on 2026-11-16) › Item 6. Extensions from a reviewed list in the Library (added on 2026-11-16) › What the person sees

Before installing, each one shows what it can do in plain words, from its permissions: "Read and change all your data on every website", "Read your browsing history", "Store data on this computer". Installing asks for an administrator's name and password, as installing a program does. Oracle › ☰ › Extensions (about:extensions) lists Ruffle (built in) and the installed ones. Each has a switch, "Allow in private windows" (off by default; never in Tor windows), Options (the extension's own settings page), Remove, its version, the Library's signature and its permissions.

docs.h: Oracle: find, closed tabs, passwords, blocking, reader mode and extensions (asked for on 2026-11-16) › Item 6. Extensions from a reviewed list in the Library (added on 2026-11-16) › What the person sees
docs.t: A puzzle button 🧩 at the right of Oracle's toolbar lists the extensions with buttons. Pressing one opens its pop-up (uBlock's per-site switch, Bitwarden's vault) under the button, as in Chrome. Each extension can be pinned next to the address box. Where it works: - Standard and Native: both, alike (Oracle on Native is the same Chromium shell, compared by same_oracle_t.sh). - Lite (WebKit): WebKitGTK cannot run Chromium's extensions, so the page says "Extensions work with the Standard and Native desktops" and the 🧩 button is not shown. - The frames fallback: extensions are not available.

docs.h: Oracle: find, closed tabs, passwords, blocking, reader mode and extensions (asked for on 2026-11-16) › Item 6. Extensions from a reviewed list in the Library (added on 2026-11-16) › How
docs.t: 1. The Library builds them (rudolfos-library): Each extension is a package apps/oext-<name>/ whose PKGINFO has type oext, the upstream repository and the pinned tag and commit, its licence, and the permissions as reviewed. The workflow fetches that exact commit, builds it with the project's own build steps (no prebuilt files from a store), and checks that the manifest's permissions are those in PKGINFO. A new permission fails the build until someone reviews it and PKGINFO says so. It packs a CRX3, includes the licence files, signs the package with the Library's key as every Library package is, and publishes it. 2. The extension's own signing key.

docs.h: Oracle: find, closed tabs, passwords, blocking, reader mode and extensions (asked for on 2026-11-16) › Item 6. Extensions from a reviewed list in the Library (added on 2026-11-16) › How
docs.t: Chromium identifies an extension by the key its CRX is signed with. Each Oracle extension needs its own key, so its ID never changes between versions. tools) and keeps them only in rudolfos-library's secrets (OEXT_KEY_<NAME>) and the owner's offline backup, as the Library's key is kept. Claude never makes, sees or handles them. Only the extension IDs (public) go in the repositories. 3. Installing on the computer (rudolfd, Chromium's managed policies): The App Store installs the package with rpk, which checks the Library's signature as it does for every package. An unsigned package, or one signed with another key, is refused.

docs.h: Oracle: find, closed tabs, passwords, blocking, reader mode and extensions (asked for on 2026-11-16) › Item 6. Extensions from a reviewed list in the Library (added on 2026-11-16) › How
docs.t: rudolfd then writes the computer's extension policy (/etc/chromium/policies/managed/rudolf-oext.json, as the shell's own policy is written today): - ExtensionSettings: "*" blocked, so Chromium installs nothing else, from anywhere; - each installed extension force_installed, with an update_url served by rudolfd on 127.0.0.1 (as the shell's iwa/update.json is), listing that package's CRX; - "Allow in private windows" from the account's choice. Chromium installs and updates extensions from that local URL only, never from Google. Removing an extension takes it out of the policy and the package is deleted. The policy is per computer, as the browser is, so extensions are installed by an administrator for everyone. Each account can turn an installed extension off for itself.

docs.h: Oracle: find, closed tabs, passwords, blocking, reader mode and extensions (asked for on 2026-11-16) › Item 6. Extensions from a reviewed list in the Library (added on 2026-11-16) › How
docs.t: Ruffle stays as it is (--load-extension, built in). 4. In Oracle's tabs. Each extension's content scripts must run in Oracle's real tabs (the shell's controlledframe), as Ruffle's do today. Check this for each one at its review: what runs, what does not, and what the extension needs from the browser's UI. The 🧩 pop-ups open the extension's chrome-extension://ID/popup.html in a small Oracle pop-up window of the shell. If a controlledframe cannot load an extension's page, it opens in a Chromium app window instead, on Standard and on Native. An extension's own toolbar badge (uBlock's count) shows on its pinned button. 5. Updates.

docs.h: Oracle: find, closed tabs, passwords, blocking, reader mode and extensions (asked for on 2026-11-16) › Item 6. Extensions from a reviewed list in the Library (added on 2026-11-16) › How
docs.t: A new version is a new Library package. Its permissions are reviewed again, and a new permission needs the administrator's approval at update time, as Chrome disables an extension until its new permissions are accepted. rpk's update installs it and rudolfd's update_url offers the new CRX. Chromium picks it up at its next check, or at once when rudolfd asks it to (if Chromium 158 has no way, at Oracle's next start). Library's revocation list (revoked.txt) applies: a revoked extension is removed from the policy at the next check, with a notification saying why. 6. Security.

docs.h: Oracle: find, closed tabs, passwords, blocking, reader mode and extensions (asked for on 2026-11-16) › Item 6. Extensions from a reviewed list in the Library (added on 2026-11-16) › How
docs.t: No extension can be installed by a website, a Linux app, a file or a non-administrator. The policy is written only by rudolfd as root, and "*" stays blocked. Extensions never run in Tor windows. In private windows they run only when allowed. Extensions never get Rudolf's system API. They live in Chromium's profile like any extension, and rudolfd refuses their requests as it refuses every program that is not the desktop (Part 10). This item gets its own security review, as item 4 does: the build's reproducibility, the permission check, the policy file, and the update path.

docs.t: 1. The mechanism, with Rudolf's own small test extension: the Library package type, CRX building and signing, the policy with everything else blocked, about:extensions, the 🧩 button and pop-ups, Standard and Native. 2. The five extensions above, each reviewed (licence, permissions, what works in a controlledframe) and published. 3. Perhaps, later and only if the owner decides: "Allow extensions from the Chrome Web Store", for an administrator, in Developer mode only, with a plain warning that Rudolf has not reviewed them. Its extensions are then still installed through the same policy, by their IDs.

docs.h: Secure Boot
docs.t: Rudolf OS 1.2.2 starts on UEFI computers with Secure Boot on. This page says how, and what to do when a part of it has to change.

docs.h: Secure Boot › The chain
docs.t: | Step | File on the disc's UEFI image | Checked by | Signed with | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | EFI/BOOT/BOOTX64.EFI, shim (Ubuntu's shim-signed) | the firmware (Microsoft's UEFI CA, in every PC) | Microsoft | | 2 | EFI/BOOT/grubx64.efi, systemd-boot: the boot menu | shim: the key enrolled in its key list (MOK) | the Rudolf OS key | | 3 | EFI/rudolf/rudolf.efi, the kernel bundle: systemd's stub, the kernel with its initramfs, fixed options | shim, through systemd-boot | the Rudolf OS key | | 3r | EFI/rudolf/recovery.efi (1.5.9), the official recovery start-up file, started by the menu's Recovery mode: the same kernel and a second initramfs in the bundle (the recovery mark and the official release key alone); it starts only system/r on RUDOLFDATA after checking its signed release list with that key and every file's size and SHA-256 (never Developer mode's extra key) | shim, through systemd-boot | the Rudolf OS key | | 4 | the system layers (RUDOLF/*.SFS) | dm-verity, against the root hashes in the signed release list RUDOLF/MANIFEST.TXT | the release key (Ed25519) | | 5 | an updated kernel in a slot on RUDOLFDATA (kexec) | the running kernel: the Rudolf

docs.h: Secure Boot › The chain
docs.t: OS certificate is built in as trusted | the Rudolf OS key | MokManager (EFI/BOOT/mmx64.efi) is where a person enrolls the Rudolf OS key the first time (EFI/rudolf/rudolf.cer), or confirms the request made by Settings > Security Settings > Prepare Secure Boot (rudolfd: POST /api/secureboot/prepare, MokNew and MokAuth with a one-time password).

docs.h: Secure Boot › The chain
docs.t: With Secure Boot on, the initramfs locks the kernel down (integrity) before anything else runs: unsigned modules (all modules are signed when the kernel is built, with a key made for that build), unsigned kernels (kexec) and writing to kernel memory are refused. A layer that fails its check, or a missing signed list, stops the start-up with a restart instead of a shell. rudolfd ignores the desktop page on RUDOLFDATA (os/current), which nothing checks. The boot menu's options are not taken from the menu (the stub ignores them under Secure Boot); the initramfs reads which entry was chosen from the firmware variable LoaderEntrySelected and adds the matching option (rudolf.recovery=1, rudolf.check=1, rudolf.toram=1; rudolf.debug=1 only with Secure Boot off).

docs.h: Secure Boot › The chain
docs.t: With Secure Boot off everything works as before, and the layers are still checked: a damaged one is caught, but an unchecked one may start (Task Manager > System says so). BIOS computers start as before (Rudolf Boot). 32-bit UEFI computers are not supported with Secure Boot on.

docs.h: Secure Boot › Keys
docs.t: Rudolf OS Secure Boot key (RSA-2048): made by iso/systools/mksbkey.sh on the maintainer's computer. iso/boot/sb/rudolf-sb.crt. The release build checks that they match (systools/sbkeycheck.py). If the key is ever replaced, every computer must enroll the new certificate (MokManager) before it starts with Secure Boot on. keys in iso/trusted-keys.txt.

docs.h: Secure Boot › Keeping shim current
docs.t: The parts a disc ships are pinned in iso/boot/sb/parts.txt and kept in the draft release sb-parts by the workflow *Secure Boot parts*. Microsoft revokes old shims from time to time (SBAT and the firmware's revocation list); a disc with a revoked shim no longer starts with Secure Boot on. Then: run *Secure Boot parts*, check the new versions in sb-parts.txt of that release, put the new hashes in parts.txt, and make a new disc. Rudolf OS's own SBAT line (rudolf,1, in systools/mkuki.py) is raised if a Rudolf OS kernel bundle must be withdrawn.

docs.h: System reports
docs.t: How a problem reported from Rudolf OS reaches this repository, and how to work with it.

docs.h: System reports › The path of a report
docs.t: 1. On the computer. The person chooses *Report a problem*: Task Manager (bottom right), or Start › Report a problem. They give it a title and say what happened; *Include the system report* is on by default.

docs.h: System reports › The path of a report
docs.t: 2. The system report (sysReport() in desktop/tm26.js) describes the computer at that moment: - Status: Rudolf OS version and installed release, when the report was made, how the computer started (BIOS or UEFI; disc, USB drive or hard disk; live or installed; recovery), whether the desktop runs in the shell or in the plain page (and whether the shell failed), the display mode and size, uptime and load, CPU use, memory and swap, temperature, battery, free storage, network connected or not, the services, open windows and real tabs, and the number of kernel warnings. - Computer: machine and firmware, processor, graphics card and driver, sound cards, storage, network adapters (kind, state, speed), input devices. - Kernel: version, start-up options, drivers, memory in detail. - Processes: the ten using the most memory, the busiest, and the memory of each page (desktop, tabs). - Latest: kernel warnings and errors, the session log, the shell's notes, the desktop's errors.

docs.h: System reports › The path of a report
docs.t: It leaves out what identifies the person: account names, file names, web addresses, network (IP) and hardware (MAC) addresses, e-mail addresses and Wi-Fi network names. The person can read it before sending (*See the report*), save it to C:\DOCUMENTS instead, or leave it out.

docs.h: System reports › The path of a report
docs.t: 3. GitHub. *Continue on GitHub* opens a new issue in Oracle (real tabs keep the GitHub sign-in) with the form .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/system-report.yml filled in through the address: title, *What happened*, version, *Status at the time* and *Full system report*. GitHub refuses very long addresses, so when the full report does not fit, Rudolf OS puts it on the clipboard and the form says to paste it. The person reviews and submits; nothing is sent before that. A GitHub account is needed. Without internet, the dialog says to save the report and send it later.

docs.h: System reports › The path of a report
docs.t: 4. The database. The workflow .github/workflows/system-reports.yml (script .github/scripts/system-reports.js) runs for every issue labelled system-report when it is opened, edited, closed or reopened, and files it in the system-reports branch: - reports/<issue>.json: the record: number, title, link, author, dates, state, version, the problem, every status line (status), and the full report text; - index.json: one line per report, newest first (state, date, version, how it started, desktop, display, memory, warnings, labels), for tools and scripts; - README.md: open reports by version and by area, and a table of all reports, to read on GitHub.

docs.h: System reports › The path of a report
docs.t: It adds labels (version: 1.2.0, area: sound, area: shell when the shell failed, needs: system report when the status is missing) and, for a new issue, a comment with the key status lines.

docs.h: System reports › Working with reports
docs.t: See them: the issues labelled system-report, or the system-reports branch's README for the overview. Filter by version: … and area: … labels. Address one: reply on the issue, fix the area labels if the guess was wrong, link the fix (Fixes #N in the pull request), and close it when the fix is released. Closing updates its state in the database. Missing status: the comment asks the person to paste *Task Manager › Copy system report*; editing the issue files the new text. Look across reports: index.json has every report in one file, for example curl -s https://raw.githubusercontent.com/merciless146/RudolfOS/system-reports/index.json | jq '.[] | select(.state=="open") | .desktop' | sort | uniq -c.
